## Discussion

### Factors Associated with BMI
Overall, our multiple linear regression model for predicting log(BMI) identifies several statistically significant predictors, but its explanatory power is modest ($R^2$ = 0.141) (@tbl-mlr-stat), indicating that much of the variability in BMI remains unexplained by the factors included in this analysis.

The model highlight physical activity and general health status as the strongest predictors of BMI (@fig-mlr-coefficients). Individuals who report engaging in physical activity tend to have lower BMI, while poorer self-reported health is consistently associated with higher BMI, with a clear gradient across health categories. These patterns suggest that BMI is closely tied not only to behavioral choices but also to broader overall health status. In contrast, smoking—while statistically significant—has a relatively small effect size, indicating limited practical importance despite the large sample size (@fig-mlr-coefficients). Age also plays a more nuanced role than initially suggested by the descriptive analysis. Individuals aged 35–54 have higher BMI compared to younger adults after adjustment, while no significant difference is observed for those aged 55+ (@fig-mlr-coefficients). This suggests that apparent increases in BMI with age may be driven more by associated health conditions and lifestyle factors than by age itself. Supporting this interpretation, variables such as diabetes and difficulty walking—factors not emphasized in the initial hypotheses—exhibit comparatively strong associations with BMI (@fig-mlr-coefficients), indicating that body weight may also reflect underlying health conditions and physical limitations rather than solely behavioral patterns.

Despite these insights, the model has several limitations. The relatively low $R^2$ suggests that important determinants of BMI—such as diet, socioeconomic status, and environmental influences—are not captured in this dataset. Additionally, the use of self-reported data introduces the potential for reporting bias, and the cross-sectional design prevents any causal interpretation of the observed relationships. Future work could incorporate more detailed behavioral and environmental variables, as well as longitudinal data, to better capture the complexity of BMI and improve predictive performance.


### Predicting Heart Attack
Overall, our logistic regression model for predicting the log-odds of heart disease displays much higher classification performance than random (AUC = 0.83 for the ROC) and exhibits high sensitivity and specificity for predicting whether an individual will experience heart attack (@fig-roc). The model posits that being over 55 years of age has the greatest impact on risk for heart attack, followed by having had a stroke or being between 35-54 years old (@fig-log-reg-coefficients). On the other hand, the model claims that generally having excellent and good health are the largest contributors to decreasing risk of heart disease, followed by being male or Asian (@fig-log-reg-coefficients). For the most part, the model confirmed our expectations that pre-existing health conditions (stroke, kidney disease, diabetes, smoking, skin cancer, difficulty walking, asthma, poor health) would predispose someone to heart disease. These health complications become more common with age due to general effects of aging on human biology and increased opportunity to be exposed to unhealthy conditions, which would explain the strong effect of older age on heart disease risk. However, contrary to these findings, the model forwarded that consuming alcohol decreases the odds of heart disease (@fig-log-reg-coefficients). This surprising result is supported by previous research. A prospective observational study conducted in the US from 1971 to 1987 with the National
Health and Nutrition Examination Survey found a moderate protective of alcohol consumption against coronary heart disease, though there was an upper bound for alcohol intake for females [@rehm1997alcohol]. A more recent meta-analysis study from 2010 corroborated these findings, showing that alcohol consumption resulted in changes to cardiovascular biomarkers (e.g. lipoprotein cholesterol) which were associated with decreased risk of coronary heart disease [@brien2011effect].

The model also predicted unexpected results for the influence of demographic factors on heart attack risk. Notably, it would predict that White individuals would be at greatest risk for heart disease compared to Hispanic, Black, and Asian individuals, a result that contradicts expectations that White individuals are economically and socially advantaged in health care spaces. A possible explanation for this could be bias in the data set due to different access to health care and formal diagnosis. For instance, White individuals may more regularly attend hospital check-ups and thus may have a higher rate of heart disease diagnosis.

### General
Though our MLR and logistic regression  models provide interesting insights into the factors that contribute to BMI and heart disease risk, the conclusions we can draw from these statistical approaches are restricted due to their heavy reliance on model assumptions (e.g. Normality of residuals and linearity). As such, a future study would be enhanced by incorporating algorithmic approaches (such as random forests or support vector machines) to increase predictive accuracy and potentially gain different information about these health outcomes.
